```{r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
source("source/birthday_sim.R")

birthday_sim(n = 10)
```

```{r}
birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    n = 10,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    shared_birthday = map(n, birthday_sim)
  ) |>
  unnest(shared_birthday)


birthday_results |>
  summarise(
    probability = mean(shared_birthday)
  )
```

```{r}
birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    n = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    shared_birthday = map(n, birthday_sim)
  ) |>
  unnest(shared_birthday)

birthday_summary =
  birthday_results |>
  group_by(n) |>
  summarise(
    probability = mean(shared_birthday),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
birthday_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a shared birthday",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Estimated probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Assuming independent birthdays uniformly distributed across 365 days, I ran `r n_distinct(birthday_results$iter)` simulations for each group size from `r min(birthday_summary$n)` to `r max(birthday_summary$n)`. The estimated probability of at least one shared birthday increased with group size, reaching `r round(100 * birthday_summary$probability[birthday_summary$n == 23], 1)`% for 23 people and `r round(100 * birthday_summary$probability[birthday_summary$n == 50], 1)`% for 50 people. As group size increases, the number of possible pairs grows, creating more opportunities for a shared birthday.

## Problem 2

```{r}
study_files =
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files("hw5_data/data")
  )

study_files =
  study_files |>
  mutate(
    file_path = str_c("hw5_data/data/", file_name),
    data = map(file_path, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
  )

study_files
```

```{r}
study_subjects =
  study_files |>
  mutate(
    file_name = str_replace(file_name, "\\.csv$", "")
  ) |>
  separate(
    file_name,
    into = c("arm", "subject_id"),
    sep = "_"
  ) |>
  select(arm, subject_id, data)

study_tidy =
  study_subjects |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week)
  )

study_tidy
```

```{r}
study_tidy |>
  mutate(
    arm = if_else(arm == "con", "Control", "Experimental"),
    participant = str_c(arm, "_", subject_id)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = week, y = observation, group = participant, color = arm)
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly observations by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The combined dataset includes `r nrow(study_subjects)` participants: `r sum(study_subjects$arm == "con")` in the control arm and `r sum(study_subjects$arm == "exp")` in the experimental arm. Each participant was observed over `r n_distinct(study_tidy$week)` weeks, yielding `r nrow(study_tidy)` participant-week observations. Experimental participants generally showed increasing observations over time, while control participants fluctuated without a clear sustained trend. The groups overlapped initially, but experimental observations were generally higher in later weeks. Individual variability remained evident in both arms.

## Problem 3

```{r}
source("source/sim_ttest.R")
```

```{r}
ttest_results =
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    result = map(mu, sim_ttest)
  ) |>
  unnest(result) |>
  mutate(
    reject = p.value < 0.05
  )

power_summary =
  ttest_results |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarise(
    rejection_rate = mean(reject),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

power_summary
```

```{r}
power_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Power of a one-sample t-test",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Rejection probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
estimate_summary =
  ttest_results |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarise(
    all_tests = mean(estimate),
    rejected_tests = mean(estimate[reject]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

estimate_summary
```

```{r}
estimate_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_tests:rejected_tests,
    names_to = "samples",
    values_to = "mean_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    samples = if_else(
      samples == "all_tests",
      "All tests",
      "Rejected tests only"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = mu,
      y = mean_estimate,
      color = samples
    )
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Average estimates across simulated tests",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = "Included tests"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

With sample size and standard deviation fixed, rejection probability increased as the true mean moved further from zero. At a true mean of 0, the estimated Type I error rate was `r round(100 * power_summary$rejection_rate[power_summary$mu == 0], 1)`%, close to the nominal 5% level. At a true mean of 3, estimated power was `r round(100 * power_summary$rejection_rate[power_summary$mu == 3], 1)`%, and it approached 100% for larger effects.

Across all tests, average estimates were close to the true means. At a true mean of 1, the average estimate was `r round(estimate_summary$all_tests[estimate_summary$mu == 1], 2)` across all tests, compared with `r round(estimate_summary$rejected_tests[estimate_summary$mu == 1], 2)` among rejected tests. For small positive effects, significance-based selection favors unusually large positive estimates, producing upward selection bias. As power increases, most tests are retained and the two averages converge. At a true mean of 0, two-sided rejection selects both positive and negative extremes, so the signed average remains centered near zero, subject to simulation variability.
